cover: Ten seconds. This benchmark measures transparency and the availability of research materials; it does not test whether reported findings reproduce or replicate. Official WSC banner, used at the speaker's request: https://worldstrokecongress.org/promotional-toolkit/ ; asset: https://wsc2026.kenes.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/32/2025/11/WSC-2026-banner-900x90px_v3.jpg
disclosure: Required by the congress as the second slide: nothing to disclose. Two seconds, then move on.
spark: Fifty seconds, first person. I came to stroke from imaging and neuroscience, where tools such as ITK-SNAP, DeepISLES, SPM Clinical Toolbox, ANTs, VLSM, LESYMAP and BCBtoolkit could be inspected and reused. BIDS and OpenNeuro support sharing. ATLAS v2.0 released 955 public MRIs with lesion masks; ISLES 2022 released 250 cases. These are examples, not a claim that every imaging workflow is open. Liew 2022 found that 12 of 17 ATLAS-based methods did not report public code. Open data alone is not enough. The illustration is conceptual artwork generated with OpenAI Image Generation, not a patient scan or empirical network.
crisis: Forty-five seconds. Use the National Academies' 2019 definitions. Reproducibility means obtaining consistent computational results with the original data, code, methods and analysis conditions. Replication asks whether a finding is consistent in a study collecting its own data to answer the same question. Different populations or interventions instead bear on generalizability. Transparency makes the material available for inspection; it does not itself establish successful reproduction or replication. The paired illustration is conceptual OpenAI-generated artwork, not measured findings. https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/25303/chapter/2
crisis-now: Sixty seconds. This slide shows a single endpoint, replication, in one project. SCORE directly replicated 151 of 274 claims drawn from social and behavioural science papers published in 2009-2018 (55.1%; Nature 2026). Each mark is one assessed claim; red marks meet the project's primary replication criterion. Outcomes depend on that criterion and this selected sample. This is not a stroke replication rate, nor a before/after trend. The 2015 psychology project found 35 significant replications among 97 tested for significance; its different sample and endpoint cannot establish improvement over time. Statistical power, researcher surveys and data availability measure other constructs and are not pooled here. Tyner et al. doi:10.1038/s41586-025-10078-y.
stroke-crisis: Fifty seconds. Now move from replication evidence in other disciplines to transparency in stroke. Animal-to-human translation is a generalizability problem. Trials enrolling different patients or using different interventions do not automatically test replication of the same claim. Tirofiban and subdural-haematoma trial contrasts have therefore been removed as evidence of a stroke reproducibility crisis. Access to protocols, data and code helps us investigate differences, with controlled access where patient privacy requires it. Missing public materials does not prove incorrect results. Our benchmark measures these enabling practices, not successful independent replication. Conceptual illustration generated with OpenAI Image Generation; not patient data.
method: Forty-five seconds. Audits like this exist for neurology (Rauh 2020) and cardiology (Heckerman 2025), and data requests have been tested in vascular and cognitive trials (Scutt 2020); we found none of stroke publications. The benchmark reads OpenAlex for every stroke journal article and review with a DOI since 2015 (140,281 for 2015-2025, title search), then reads up to 1,500 open-access full texts a year through Europe PMC (16,362 for stroke), with neurology, neuroscience and cardiology measured the same way. It re-runs every six months; code and data are open, and every number on the next slides is on the public dashboard: the QR code. Open-access full text only, so full-text rates run high.
oa-trend: Thirty-five seconds. The good-news slide. Open access = any OpenAlex status other than closed. Stroke sits between cardiology and neurology in every complete year (2015-2024); in the incomplete 2025 it edges past cardiology. Do not rank neuroscience: about 45% of it comes from the title term 'neural', much of it machine learning.
oa-type: Forty seconds. Gold/hybrid stroke publication routes increased from 18.6% in 2015 to 44.1% in 2024; diamond/green from 18.9% to 23.9%; bronze declined from 15.3% to 7.2%. The remaining share was closed. These classify publication routes, not observed payments. Waivers and funding agreements are not measured. The two bars each include all stroke articles in that year and sum to 100%.
who-pays: Forty-five seconds. Stroke articles, 2015-2025, high-income first-author group: 83% open access when OpenAlex lists a funder (29,055 articles), versus 56% without a listed funder (44,147). This is a descriptive association, not a causal estimate of funding. No listed funder does not prove no funding: acknowledgements may be missing. The groups may differ in year, journal and study type. Source: benchmark 2026-10-13, Income groups.
countries: Forty seconds. Selected stroke first-author countries, 2015-2025: Indonesia, Netherlands, Korea and United States. Components use the same corpus and years. These are descriptive examples, not a ranking or a causal effect of policy or wealth. Gold and hybrid often charge fees, but article-level payments, waivers and funding agreements were not observed. Diamond and green are publishing or repository routes.
flat: Thirty-five seconds. Lower bounds from abstracts and metadata, 2024: data in a repository 0.2% (0.2% in 2015, never above 0.6%); code links below 0.1% in every complete year. What did move: registration IDs, 2.8% to 5.3% of articles with an abstract, and preprints, 2.7% in 2024, partly publisher-driven (Research Square, SSRN). Pooled over 2015-2025, high-impact articles are barely better at sharing (data 0.45% vs 0.34%). Then the pivot: so we read the full text. The figure measures detected links, not the availability of all underlying data or code.
das: Sixty seconds; the slide people photograph. Open-access stroke full texts published in 2025 (the audit reads 1,500 a year, so the year is complete for the audit): 74% write a data statement (14% in 2015), 29% say 'available on request', now the most common answer, and 9.8% deposit data or name a public source (own repository deposit 5.9%). In 2024: 69%, 30% and 7.3%. 'On request' delivers little: 6.8% of authors shared when asked (Gabelica 2022); 20% of 391 vascular and cognitive trials, median 241 days (Scutt 2020). Against the other fields, 2022-2025, stroke says 'on request' most often (30%; neurology 27%, neuroscience 26%, cardiology 24%). Open-access full texts only, so these rates are optimistic for stroke overall.
equity: Forty seconds. Among the three larger income groups, lower-middle-income first authors are the most open to read (75%, 42% through diamond or green), yet in open-access full texts, 2015-2025, they write a data statement in 23% (high 43%, upper-middle 57%) and deposit or name a public source in 1.8% (4.0%, 5.2%), from 609 audited articles; the gap holds in 2022-2025. Both panels use the same scale, which is the point: deposit is tiny everywhere. Low-income countries (400 articles, 77 audited) are too few to show. Korea: 5,490 first-author articles, 75% open.
commitment: Forty-five seconds. The index is the mean, over three full-text signals (data deposited or public source, GitHub, trial registration), of an institution's rate divided by the stroke rate; 1 = stroke average. Shown: the top of the 60 institutions with the most audited articles (82 or more each), as on the dashboard. Charité is counted once: OpenAlex lists its Center for Stroke Research Berlin and the Berlin Institute of Health separately, and those are merged into it (133 audited articles; deposit or public source 9.8%, GitHub 10.5%, trial registration 37%). Small counts are a hint, not a ranking. Journals: among the 40 largest on the dashboard, the Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism leads (2.7x) and Stroke is fourth (1.5x); among smaller journals with at least 30 audited articles, Nature Communications, Brain Communications and PeerJ lead. The point: the measurement exists, is cheap, and is what a prize would recognise.
mandates: Fifty seconds. One medical example, not a pooled estimate: Bergeat et al., JAMA Network Open 2022, surgical RCTs before and after the ICMJE data-availability statement requirement. Obtainable datasets were 3.1% in both periods. This descriptive before/after comparison does not establish a causal effect. Evidence on badges, promotion criteria and Registered Reports measures other outcomes and is kept off this visual. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.15209.
future: One minute forty-five. Proposal: ask WSO to convene a task force and develop a position statement; retire 'available on request' in Stroke, IJS, ESJ and JSCVD in favour of a repository, VISTA or Vivli, or a stated reason; Registered Reports for stroke trials with in-principle acceptance tied to WSO and ESO grants; embargoed sharing as the trial default, twelve months after publication. Prize: the commitment index, verified in full text and recomputed every six months, for institutions, journals, funders and countries. Awareness: the public benchmark; open-science items in promotion criteria (in 2020, 1 of 92 guidelines mentioned data sharing, and none open access or registration). Targets to discuss: data in a repository or controlled-access platform for 25% of stroke articles by 2030 (own repository deposit was 5.9% of 2025 open-access full texts); 'on request' under 10%; one Registered Report track in a stroke journal by 2028. The statement, retiring 'on request' and promotion criteria cost nothing; Registered Reports, the prize and the infrastructure need money, and the infrastructure mostly exists: VISTA and Vivli for trial data, ATLAS and OpenNeuro for imaging, ENIGMA for pooled analysis. Invite the WSO leadership in the room to take the task force home. Proposed targets and deadlines are discussion points, not commitments or current WSO policy.
close: Thirty seconds. One line, then stop. Leave the QR codes up during questions: the benchmark dashboard, the code and data, and the references. Thank the session chairs.
